claims.text: The additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 alloy has an FCC matrix.
The initial FCC matrix is homogeneous and contains finely dispersed strengthening phases.
The strengthening phases are thermally stable at elevated temperature.
In oxidizing environments, degradation is governed by selective oxidation of aluminum and titanium at grain boundaries.
Selective oxidation produces brittle, non-adherent grain-boundary oxide phases.
The grain-boundary oxides are likely Al2O3 and TiO2.
The proposed oxide phases are non-coherent with the FCC matrix.
Aluminum and titanium preferentially oxidize near precipitate interfaces as well as at grain boundaries.
Thermal-expansion mismatch between the oxides and matrix induces localized stresses.
Localized oxide-induced stresses cause microcrack nucleation and propagation.
Oxide-induced cracking can ultimately cause catastrophic failure.
Reducing conditions significantly lower the oxidation rate and preserve mechanical integrity relative to oxidizing conditions.
Oxidizing exposure will increase grain-boundary oxide formation and microcrack density relative to the starting state.
Oxidizing exposure will reduce creep strength or tensile ductility relative to the starting state.
Reducing exposure will mitigate oxide formation and cracking and delay catastrophic failure relative to oxidizing exposure.
The proposed oxidation-controlled degradation mechanism applies above approximately 700 °C when oxygen partial pressure is high enough to promote rapid selective oxidation.
Below approximately 700 °C or at lower oxygen availability, oxidation is less severe and may not dominate degradation.

contradictions.description: The intervention specifies a comparison between oxidizing and reducing gases, but the experimental design treats either H2 or an inert gas as the reducing condition. An inert low-oxygen atmosphere is not necessarily chemically reducing, so these controls do not implement the same environmental contrast.
